children.title: Kennedy Removes All 17 Members of CDC Vaccine Advisory Panel
children.description_short: Kennedy removed all 17 members of CDC's vaccine advisory panel on June 9, 2025.
children.description_medium: On June 9, 2025, HHS Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. removed all 17 members of the CDC’s Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices and said they would be replaced. Reuters reported that vaccine scientists protested the move and that experts warned it could undermine public confidence in health agencies. This child records the panel action only; it does not describe the committee as dissolved or characterize all replacement members.
children.description_long: On June 9, 2025, Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. removed all 17 members of the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention’s Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices (ACIP). Reuters reported that Kennedy was in the process of replacing them and that many vaccine scientists protested the decision. The committee advises the CDC on how vaccines are used and by whom. Reuters also reported that the members had been appointed during the Biden administration, including 13 in 2024, and that without their removal the Trump administration would not have been able to choose a majority of the committee until 2028. Kennedy described the change as part of restoring public trust; experts quoted by Reuters said the dismissal could undermine confidence in health agencies. That is an attributed warning, not evidence that public confidence or vaccine access measurably changed. The CDC said the panel’s next meeting would take place June 25–27 in Atlanta. This record covers the June committee-removal action only. The source describes members being replaced, not ACIP being dissolved, and the supplied broad label for replacement members is not repeated. HHS’s release also describes ACIP as making recommendations on vaccine safety, efficacy, and clinical need to CDC.
organization_tags: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention
U.S. Department of Health and Human Services

Under the leadership of HHS Secretary Robert F. Kennedy, Jr., the agency removed the 17 sitting members of the ACIP committee and will replace them with new members currently under consideration.

WASHINGTON, June 9 (Reuters) - Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. has fired all 17 members of a U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention panel of vaccine experts and is in the process of replacing them, his department said on Monday, drawing protest from many vaccine scientists.

Scientists and experts said the changes to the vaccine panel, which recommends how vaccines are used and by whom, would undermine public confidence in health agencies.

All 17 ACIP members were appointed under former President Joe Biden's administration, including 13 in 2024, HHS said. Without their removal, Trump's administration would not have been able to choose a majority of the committee until 2028.

The CDC panel will convene its next meeting June 25-27 at CDC headquarters in Atlanta, the department said.

children.title: HHS Layoffs Begin at NIH During a Planned 1,200-Position Reduction
children.description_short: HHS layoffs began at NIH on April 1, 2025; the department's plan targeted about 1,200 NIH positions.
children.description_medium: HHS began broad health-agency layoffs on April 1, 2025, and Reuters reported that the National Institutes of Health was among the affected agencies, with NIH employees notified of layoffs that morning. HHS’s restructuring fact sheet separately said the plan would reduce NIH’s workforce by approximately 1,200 through centralized support functions. The plan figure is a target, not proof that exactly 1,200 people were dismissed.
children.description_long: On April 1, 2025, the Trump administration began mass layoffs across federal health agencies. Reuters reported that the cuts affected the National Institutes of Health and that NIH employees had been notified early that morning that they were laid off. HHS’s restructuring fact sheet described a planned NIH workforce reduction of approximately 1,200 employees through the centralization of procurement, human resources, and communications across its 27 institutes and centers. The figure is the department’s plan, not a verified count of completed dismissals. Reuters described a broader 10,000-person reduction across health agencies, not 10,000 NIH layoffs. The supplied February 20 entry merged this workforce action with the separate June removal of ACIP members; this child isolates the NIH-related layoffs and uses the April 1 date. The source material does not establish that hundreds of the affected NIH workers were scientists, identify the number of researchers who lost jobs, or measure any resulting research interruption. It also does not show that all planned NIH reductions occurred. The record therefore describes the confirmed start of layoffs and the department’s stated target separately, without converting the target into an outcome.

children.title: DOJ and FBI Say Their Epstein Review Found No Incriminating Client List
children.description_short: DOJ and FBI Say Their Epstein Review Found No Incriminating Client List
children.description_medium: On July 7, 2025, the Justice Department and FBI released a memorandum describing a review of investigative holdings relating to Jeffrey Epstein. The agencies said the review found no incriminating “client list,” no credible evidence Epstein blackmailed prominent individuals, and no evidence to predicate an investigation of uncharged third parties. The memorandum says victim privacy and court seals limited disclosure.
children.description_long: The Justice Department and FBI’s July 7, 2025 memorandum described a review of investigative holdings relating to Jeffrey Epstein and the agencies’ decision about further disclosure. It said FBI personnel searched digital systems and physical storage locations, then had agents, analysts, attorneys, and privacy and civil-liberties experts review the material. The agencies said the files included images and videos involving minors and identifying information about victims; it also said much of the material was subject to court-ordered sealing. The memorandum stated that the review found no incriminating “client list,” no credible evidence Epstein blackmailed prominent individuals, and no evidence that could predicate an investigation of uncharged third parties. It described Epstein as having harmed more than one thousand victims and said no further disclosure was appropriate or warranted. These are the government’s stated conclusions about its review; the memorandum does not say every person associated with Epstein was investigated or exonerated. This record covers the July review and its public findings alone. It does not treat the memo as proof of the separate birthday-message dispute or the later DOJ investigation request.

children.title: Trump Sues Wall Street Journal over Epstein Birthday-Note Report
children.description_short: Trump sued the Wall Street Journal over its report about a 2003 Epstein birthday greeting.
children.description_medium: Reuters reported that Trump filed a defamation suit on July 18, 2025, seeking at least $10 billion from the Wall Street Journal and related defendants over its report about a 2003 birthday greeting to Jeffrey Epstein. Trump denied the report, and Reuters said it had not verified the underlying account. The suit’s allegations were not a court finding.
children.description_long: Reuters reported that President Donald Trump filed a defamation suit on July 18, 2025, against the Wall Street Journal and its owners, including Rupert Murdoch, seeking at least $10 billion. The lawsuit followed the newspaper’s report that Trump’s name appeared on a 2003 birthday greeting for Jeffrey Epstein with a sexually suggestive drawing and a reference to secrets they shared. Reuters said the complaint alleged that the story defamed Trump and caused financial and reputational harm. Trump denied the Journal’s account, and Reuters stated that it had not independently verified the underlying report. This record treats the filing as a confirmed legal action and the birthday message as an allegation in reporting that Trump disputed. A complaint’s allegations do not establish defamation, and a reported denial does not resolve whether the message existed or who wrote it. The suit is a separate July event from the Justice Department and FBI’s review memorandum and from the later announcement that federal prosecutors would examine Epstein’s ties to political figures. This description does not imply any court ruling or final result in the case.

children.title: Trump Requests Epstein-Ties Inquiry; DOJ Assigns Jay Clayton
children.description_short: Trump requested a DOJ inquiry into Epstein’s ties to Clinton and others; Bondi assigned Jay Clayton.
children.description_medium: Reuters reported on November 14, 2025, that the Justice Department would fulfill Trump’s request to investigate Jeffrey Epstein’s ties to Bill Clinton and JPMorgan. Attorney General Pam Bondi said Manhattan U.S. Attorney Jay Clayton would lead the inquiry; Trump also named Larry Summers and Reid Hoffman. The report describes an announced investigation, not charges or findings against the people named.
children.description_long: On November 14, 2025, Reuters reported that the Justice Department would fulfill President Donald Trump’s request to investigate Jeffrey Epstein’s ties to former President Bill Clinton and JPMorgan. Attorney General Pam Bondi said Jay Clayton, the top federal prosecutor in Manhattan, would lead the investigation. Reuters reported that Trump also asked the department to examine former Treasury Secretary Larry Summers and Reid Hoffman, and that all three men had been mentioned in documents released by the House Oversight Committee. The article said the department’s decision came despite a July memorandum in which DOJ and the FBI said they had found no evidence that could predicate an investigation against uncharged third parties. Reuters characterized Trump as seeking to shift attention from his own relationship with Epstein and noted that the inquiry could face a challenge as vindictive prosecution; these are attributed reporting and analysis, not judicial findings. This record covers the request and announced assignment only. It does not say that charges were filed, that investigators reached conclusions, or that the named individuals committed wrongdoing.

children.title: Paramount Settles Trump’s 60 Minutes Lawsuit for $16 Million
children.description_short: Paramount agreed to pay $16 million to settle Trump’s lawsuit over a 60 Minutes interview; the settlement did not establish that the interview was improperly edited.
children.description_medium: On July 2, 2025, Paramount agreed to pay $16 million to settle Donald Trump’s lawsuit over a 60 Minutes interview with Kamala Harris. PBS NewsHour reported that Trump alleged the interview was edited to improve how Harris sounded, which CBS denied. Paramount said the money would go to Trump’s future presidential library and that CBS would not issue an apology. PBS also reported that Paramount was seeking merger approval from the Trump administration; concerns about a connection were reported as allegations, not proven as an exchange.
children.description_long: On July 2, 2025, Paramount agreed to pay Donald Trump $16 million to settle his lawsuit over a 60 Minutes interview with then-Vice President Kamala Harris. Trump alleged that the interview had been edited to improve how Harris sounded; CBS denied the allegation. Paramount said the payment would go to the president’s future library and that the settlement did not require an apology. The case therefore ended in a payment, not a court finding that CBS had manipulated the interview. PBS NewsHour’s report also described a separate context: Paramount was seeking administration approval for its proposed Skydance merger, and interview guest Brian Stelter said that was why the word “bribe” had come up in public discussion. Paramount and the FCC denied that suggestion. The reporting does not establish that merger review was exchanged for the settlement or that the administration conditioned approval on payment. This entry records the settlement and the attributed concern without treating coercion as a proven fact. Other incidents in the original card are handled separately.

children.title: Trump Signs Rescission Cutting About $1.1 Billion for Public Broadcasting
children.description_short: Trump signed a rescission bill that canceled about $1.1 billion allocated to the Corporation for Public Broadcasting, according to AP reporting published by PBS.
children.description_medium: On July 24, 2025, President Donald Trump signed a bill canceling about $9 billion in previously approved foreign-aid and public-broadcasting spending. The Associated Press, published by PBS NewsHour, said about $1.1 billion was allocated to the Corporation for Public Broadcasting, which finances NPR and PBS, with most of that amount distributed to more than 1,500 local stations. The bill was enacted; this report does not document later station-level effects.
children.description_long: On July 24, 2025, President Donald Trump signed a rescission bill that canceled about $9 billion in previously approved spending for public broadcasting and foreign aid. The Associated Press reported through PBS NewsHour that about $1.1 billion had been allocated to the Corporation for Public Broadcasting, which financed NPR and PBS; most of that amount was distributed to more than 1,500 local public radio and television stations. The article describes a completed federal rescission, not merely a proposed cut. It says the White House had presented the bill as a test case for additional rescission packages and reports that Democrats unanimously opposed it but could not stop it. This card is limited to the signed rescission and the reported funding channel. It does not claim that the entire $1.1 billion would have gone directly to NPR or PBS, that every local station lost the same amount, or that specific station closures followed. The original record grouped this measure with separate legal disputes, media criticism, FCC inquiries, and immigration enforcement; those actions are not part of this dated entry.

children.title: White House Media Page Labels News Outlets as “Offenders”
children.description_short: By Dec. 3, 2025, a White House webpage labeled selected outlets and reports as media “offenders,” according to Reporters Without Borders.
children.description_medium: By December 3, 2025, the White House maintained a webpage labeling selected news coverage and outlets as media “offenders.” Reporters Without Borders described sections called “Media Offender of the Week,” “Hall of Shame,” and a leaderboard; it reported that CBS News, The Boston Globe, and The Independent appeared in the first section. RSF said the page offered no factual breakdown for its accusations. This entry documents the page’s existence and reported structure without adopting its accusations or RSF’s broader evaluation as established fact.
children.description_long: A Reporters Without Borders report dated December 3, 2025, described an official White House media-bias page that labeled selected outlets and reports “offenders.” It said the “Media Offender of the Week” section then named CBS News, The Boston Globe, and The Independent, and that the site also maintained a “Hall of Shame” and a leaderboard ranking outlets it alleged had reported inaccurately. RSF said the page supplied no factual breakdown for why its accusations were correct and urged the White House to remove it. This card records the existence and structure of the government page without endorsing the page’s claims or treating RSF’s criticism as a legal finding. December 3 is the date RSF described the page, not a verified launch date. The original entry grouped this page with separate settlements, appropriations, FCC investigations, and an immigration case; those incidents require their own dated sourcing and are not inferred from the webpage.
